(ID1484-021){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |title=Misumi West Port |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154649/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }}{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223154759/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-date=23 December 2019 |title=三角旧港（三角西港）施設 |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=17 February 2012 }} || constructed in 1887, {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}} || [[File:Misumi-West-port Uki Kumamoto.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Area 8: Yahata in Fukuoka== {{ill|Yahata Steel Works|en|Yahata Steel Works|WD=Q2943310|lt=Yawata steel works|1=Yahata Steel Works}}; [[:en:Kitakyūshū, Fukuoka|Kitakyūshū]] and {{ill|Nakama, Fukuoka|en|Nakama, Fukuoka|WD=Q847601|lt=Nakama|1=Nakama, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !colspan="2" width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| image |- |colspan="2" width="40%" | {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works, Japan|[[:ja:官営八幡製鐵所|旧官営八幡製鐵所関連施設]]|kyū kanei Yahata seitetsusho kanren shisetsu}}
(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by {{ill|Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|en|Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|WD=Q1197264|lt=METI|1=Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry}}. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-jimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repairing factory|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho syūzen-kōjou}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Metalsmith factory|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjou}} | constructed in 1900 | |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima_Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites arraised concerns and objections from {{ill|South Korea|en|South Korea|WD=Q884|lt=South Korea|1=South Korea}}, on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}} mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[:en:World Heritage Sites in Japan|World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * {{ill|Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region|en|Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region|WD=Q93643|lt=Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region|1=Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region}} ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * industrialization of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}} in the {{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Bakumatsu|1=Bakumatsu}} and {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji|1=Meiji era}} periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the {{ill|industrial heritage|en|industrial heritage|WD=Q1569871|lt=industrial heritage|1=Industrial heritage}} of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher={{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the {{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} [[:en:World Heritage List|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cn|date=July 2020}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[:en:Tokugawa period|Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; {{ill|Hagi, Yamaguchi|en|Hagi, Yamaguchi|WD=Q378225|lt=Hagi|1=Hagi, Yamaguchi}}, {{ill|Yamaguchi Prefecture|en|Yamaguchi Prefecture|WD=Q127264|lt=Yamaguchi Prefecture|1=Yamaguchi Prefecture}}: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| image |- | {{nihongo|{{ill|Hagi Reverberatory Furnace|en|Hagi Reverberatory Furnace|WD=Q20637540|lt=Hagi Reverberatory Furnace|1=Hagi Reverberatory Furnace}}|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-021){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |title=Misumi West Port |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154649/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }}{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223154759/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-date=23 December 2019 |title=三角旧港（三角西港）施設 |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=17 February 2012 }} || constructed in 1887, {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}} || [[File:Misumi-West-port Uki Kumamoto.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Area 8: Yahata in Fukuoka== {{ill|Yahata Steel Works|en|Yahata Steel Works|WD=Q2943310|lt=Yawata steel works|1=Yahata Steel Works}}; [[:en:Kitakyūshū, Fukuoka|Kitakyūshū]] and {{ill|Nakama, Fukuoka|en|Nakama, Fukuoka|WD=Q847601|lt=Nakama|1=Nakama, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !colspan="2" width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| image |- |colspan="2" width="40%" | {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works, Japan|[[:ja:官営八幡製鐵所|旧官営八幡製鐵所関連施設]]|kyū kanei Yahata seitetsusho kanren shisetsu}}
(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by {{ill|Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|en|Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|WD=Q1197264|lt=METI|1=Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry}}. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-jimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repairing factory|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho syūzen-kōjou}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Metalsmith factory|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjou}} | constructed in 1900 | |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima_Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites arraised concerns and objections from {{ill|South Korea|en|South Korea|WD=Q884|lt=South Korea|1=South Korea}}, on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}} mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[:en:World Heritage Sites in Japan|World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * {{ill|Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region|en|Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region|WD=Q93643|lt=Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region|1=Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region}} ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * {{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-021){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |title=Misumi West Port |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154649/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }}{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223154759/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-date=23 December 2019 |title=三角旧港（三角西港）施設 |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=17 February 2012 }} || constructed in 1887, [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Property]] || [[File:Misumi-West-port Uki Kumamoto.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Area 8: Yahata in Fukuoka== [[Yahata Steel Works|Yawata steel works]]; [[Kitakyūshū, Fukuoka|Kitakyūshū]] and [[Nakama, Fukuoka|Nakama]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !colspan="2" width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- |colspan="2" width="40%" | {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works, Japan|[[:ja:官営八幡製鐵所|旧官営八幡製鐵所関連施設]]|kyū kan'ei Yahata seitetsusho kanren shisetsu}}
(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-021){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |title=Misumi West Port |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154649/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }}{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223154759/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-date=23 December 2019 |title=三角旧港（三角西港）施設 |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=17 February 2012 }} || constructed in 1887, [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Property]] || [[File:Misumi-West-port Uki Kumamoto.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Area 8: Yahata in Fukuoka== [[Yahata Steel Works|Yawata steel works]]; [[Kitakyūshū, Fukuoka|Kitakyūshū]] and [[Nakama, Fukuoka|Nakama]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !colspan="2" width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- |colspan="2" width="40%" | {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works, Japan|[[:ja:官営八幡製鐵所|旧官営八幡製鐵所関連施設]]|kyū kan'ei Yahata seitetsusho kanren shisetsu}}
(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-021){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |title=Misumi West Port |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154649/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_miike_04.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }}{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223154759/https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3773 |archive-date=23 December 2019 |title=三角旧港（三角西港）施設 |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=17 February 2012 }} || constructed in 1887, [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Property]] || [[File:Misumi-West-port Uki Kumamoto.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Area 8: Yahata in Fukuoka== [[Yahata Steel Works|Yawata steel works]]; [[Kitakyūshū, Fukuoka|Kitakyūshū]] and [[Nakama, Fukuoka|Nakama]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !colspan="2" width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- |colspan="2" width="40%" | {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works, Japan|[[:ja:官営八幡製鐵所|旧官営八幡製鐵所関連施設]]|kyū kan'ei Yahata seitetsusho kanren shisetsu}}
(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}

(ID1484-022){{cite web |url=http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |title=The State-owned Yawata Steel Works |publisher=Kyuyama |access-date=17 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016154751/http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/kyushuyamaguchi/ky_yawata_01.html |archive-date=16 October 2013 }} | establishing political decision was made in 1897, started operation in 1901, "Heritage of Industrial Modernization" by [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry|METI]]. | [[File:Governmental Yawata Iron & Steel Works.JPG|250px]] |- |rowspan="3" style="border-top:hidden"| |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: First Head Office|八幡製鐵所 旧本事務所|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-honjimusyo}} | constructed in 1899 | [[File:八幡製鉄所旧本事務所.JPG|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Repair Shop|八幡製鐵所 修繕工場|Yahata seitetsusho shūzen-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900, the oldest steel structure in Japan, still under operation. | [[File:修繕工場西面外観.png|250px]] |- |width="20%"| {{nihongo|The Imperial Steel Works: Former Forge Shop|八幡製鐵所 旧鍛冶工場|Yahata seitetsusho kyū-kaji-kōjō}} | constructed in 1900 | [[File:旧鍛冶工場東面外観.png|250px]] |- |colspan="2" | {{nihongo|Onga river Pumping Station|[[:ja:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室|遠賀川水源地ポンプ室]]|Onga-gawa suigenchi ponpu-shitsu}}
(ID1484-023) | constructed in 1910, still under operation. |[[File:遠賀川水源地ポンプ室１.JPG|250px]] |- |} ==Controversy== {{Main|Hashima Island#World Heritage Site approval controversy}} The inclusion of some of these properties as UNESCO Heritage sites raised concerns and objections from [[South Korea]], on the grounds that conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners-of-war were forced to work under harsh conditions at seven of these sites during Japan's [[World War II]] mobilization policies. There is a research questioning about Japanese government's compliance with UNESCO regulations and requirements with respect to Hashima Coal Mine site.{{cite journal |last=Palmer |first=David |date=January 1, 2018 |title=Gunkanjima / Battleship Island, Nagasaki: World Heritage Historical Site or Urban Ruins Tourist Attraction? |url=https://apjjf.org/2018/01/Palmer.html |journal=The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus |volume=16 |issue=1 |access-date=July 4, 2020}} Although the period at which forced labour took place does not coincide with the period of Meiji industrial revolution, the criticism arose based on the view that the Meiji industrial revolution was "inseparable from 20th-century empire-building, which led inexorably to Japanese colonialism and the Asia-Pacific War".{{cite news | title = Story of Japan's industrial rise deserves to be told, forced labor and all | url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2015/06/24/voices/story-japans-industrial-rise-deserves-told-forced-labor/ | access-date=2020-07-05 | work=The Japan Times | date=2015-06-24}} South Korea claimed that the official recognition of those sites would "violate the dignity of the survivors of forced labor as well as the spirit and principles of the UNESCO Convention", and "World Heritage sites should be of outstanding universal value and be acceptable by all peoples across the globe." China also released a similar statement that "World Heritage application should live up to the principle and spirit of promoting peace as upheld by UNESCO." ==See also== * [[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] * [[Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== * [https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5399/ UNESCO Tentative List entry] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/index.html The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/e/action/teigensyoE.pdf Emergence of Industrial Japan: Kyushu and Yamaguchi] * [http://www.kyuyama.jp/ The Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi] {{in lang|ja}} * [https://www.ihic.jp/ Industrial Heritage Information Center] {{in lang|ja}} {{Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining}} {{World Heritage Sites in Japan}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Modern Industrial Heritage Sites in Kyushu and Yamaguchi}} [[Category:Anti-Japanese sentiment in Korea]] [[Category:Bakumatsu]] [[Category:Meiji era]] [[Category:Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Saga Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamaguchi Prefecture]] [[Category:Industrial archaeological sites]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]

{{Short description|UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan}} {{Infobox UNESCO World Heritage Site | image = Hagi Castle Town Aerial photograph.1976.jpg | image_upright = 1.2 | caption = Aerial photograph of [[Hagi Castle]] Town | location = [[Japan]] | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii), (iv)}}(ii), (iv) | ID = 1484 | coordinates = {{coord|34|25|50|N|131|24|44|E|display=title, inline|format=dms}} | year = 2015 | area = {{convert|306.66|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|2,408.33|ha|acre|abbr=on}} | locmapin = World | map_caption = }} {{nihongo|'''Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'''|明治日本の産業革命遺産 製鉄・鉄鋼、造船、石炭産業|Meiji nihon no sangyōkakumei isan: seitetsu, tekkō, zōsen, sekitan sangyō}} are a group of historic sites that played an important part in the industrialization of [[Japan]] in the [[Bakumatsu]] and [[Meiji era|Meiji]] periods (1850s–1910), and are part of the [[industrial heritage]] of Japan.{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1484/|title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=5 July 2015}} In 2009 the monuments were submitted jointly for inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Sites|World Heritage List]] under criteria [[World Heritage Site#Cultural criteria|ii, iii, and iv]]. The sites were accepted at the 39th UNESCO World Heritage session, under the condition to take measures "that allow an understanding that there were a large number of Koreans and others who were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions ...", and again, such measures have yet to be implemented.{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ5lR7Cj5C8| title=Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, "Unfulfilled Promises" | website=[[YouTube]] }} Eight areas are registered, with twenty-three component sites:{{cite web |url=https://www.japansmeijiindustrialrevolution.com/en/site/index.html |title=Story and sites | publisher=Japans Meiji IndustrialRevolution | access-date=5 January 2025}} ==Area 1: Hagi in Yamaguchi== Hagi proto-industrial sites and [[Tokugawa period]] cultural setting; [[Hagi, Yamaguchi|Hagi]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]: {| class="wikitable sortable" width="100%" style="background:#ffffff;" |- !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" | Site !width="40%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Comments !width="20%" align="left" style="background:#ffdead;" class="unsortable"| Image |- | {{nihongo|[[Hagi Reverberatory Furnace]]|萩反射炉|Hagi hansharo}}
